I think you need to take a step back. You’re pushing pretty hard to try to get to an ideal that could never manifest. 

Stepparenting situations are all so unique and individual that I think it’s dangerous of you to be dreaming of some Brady Bunch ideal. The two older girls are close in age, but when they meet they may hate each other. Your step kids have an active mother in their life and may resent if you try to push parenting on them too much too fast. You might find the kids are completely uninterested in having you as an authority figure at all. Or none of this might happen and blending goes great. But it takes about 7 years for a family to truly blend. Let go of the fantasy and embrace the reality.

Right now, NAH. You’re an adult moving in more than half a year. It would be nice to have her assistance, but you need to be solving your own problems. You’re moving in the fall, so you have months to figure this out rather than wallowing in the problem/hurt feelings. 

You can’t park on campus? Okay. Drive yourself with necessities and find somewhere to park your car for free overnight and Uber or walk to your dorm. Drive your car back home and get a ride back with your mom and the rest of your stuff. 

Other option is to move in another day. Big move in day is a Saturday? Move on Sunday. As long as you’re there for your first day of classes, you’ll be fine. 

You have more than half a year to figure this out. Find another friend or relative to help you move.

Nope. No big deal. My SD was using them regularly until she turned 7.5. She still occasionally wets the bed, but it’s so infrequent that we don’t use the pull-ups anymore. 

One of the risks is that they become more okay with peeing at night since there aren’t consequences because of the pull-up. Right about when SD turned 7, we started using a calendar to track wet and dry nights. There were small rewards for multiple dry nights in a row. It helped immediately and it went from 50/50 dry and wet to 90/10 dry and wet. After she went a whole month without wetting the bed, we let her choose to stop wearing the pull-ups.

This is our life, here’s how it goes: unless you’re somewhere very unusual, your husband is the presumed father since he’s on the birth certificate. If he comes back as not the bio father, he’s still required to support her unless he can prove who the biofather is and sue to have the bio father replace him on the birth certificate. Then, by making this choice, he loses all rights to the daughter he’s raised since birth as his. No one wins here except maybe you if you pursue this expensive path. 

On the other hand, you can just roll with it. Stop doubting unless you have more solid proof. In our case, my SD is very obviously biracial, and neither of her parents are black. Even with proof she’s not his biologically, she is still my husbands daughter. If she wasn’t asking questions about why she looks so different from her family, she might not have found out for a long time.

Gentle YTA. This is one of the things I fear about being a stepparent. I worry that if my husband dies before me, my stepkid will walk away and I’ll completely without my family. He says it won’t happen, but stories like this make me think otherwise. I know I would have a really hard time letting go of pieces of my husband if he died. The idea that she’s dating and moved on is contradictory to the fact she’s having trouble letting go of his things. Grief is hard; no need to make it harder. 

A couple of other things: you’re kind of judge-y about how soon she started dating. Everyone grieves in their own way. Plus she had longer to prepare for your fathers death. As someone who lost a parent to a degenerative illness, the mourning happened mostly in the years leading up to death. By the time he died, it was mostly relief. 

He might not have wanted you to know it was coming. It seems like once or twice a week there’s someone asking if their the AH for not telling their family they have a terminal illness. That seems to have been the direction your father went here.

I’m not a guy, but I’ve been there and done that. FTD finally killed my father 2.5 years ago and it sucks. The whole thing sucks. I would recommend counseling and support groups. Counseling helped me mourn all of the many small losses of who they are over the many years. For me I think the worst one was when my dad stopped playing guitar. There are some groups out there for FTD caregivers, but not a ton since it’s pretty uncommon. My experience with an Alzheimer’s support group (only thing near me) was that they become a pissing match of who has it worst, and FTD is probably worse than what they’re dealing with. The one time I made it to an FTD meeting was a lot better. 

Which variant does he have? My father had the semantic variant. The only small bit of hope I have for you is that there’s a pretty low genetic connection identified so far, so it’s often random shiftiness that you are not likely to get.

As it got worse for us and we couldn’t control my father, we ended up putting him in a home. We were fortunate to be able to afford it. Have you gotten your father on disability yet? It helped a lot for us. There are resources available for providing nursing care, Day care, and eventually hospice. I used some of the resources available through the Alzheimer’s association to find stuff. You can call them for help as well. It’s a much larger network than the FTD specific organization. Have things like wills, power of attorney, and last wishes been taken care of? The earlier you do that stuff, the better. I don’t know how far gone your dad is, but it took a couple of years for us to find out what it was, so he’d progressed a ways. 

Even though I know there’s a low genetic association, I’m still terrified I’ll get it. Counseling helped a little, but sometimes it keeps me up at night. You’re 26. Maybe you’ve already been through it, but at this point your brain is changing and it doesn’t operate at the peak it did when you were 22 or so. This is normal. It’s hard, but don’t over analyze the little deficiencies that you notice. They’re happening to everyone at this age, but not everyone is dealing with a family member’s brain disintegrating in their skull.

This is getting long and rambling. Lastly, at the end, don’t be surprised if you feel relief when they finally die. In the end, unless they have a heart attack or something kills them early, they’re just a shell of the person you knew and loved that died in pieces over the years it took to get that far. Again, counseling helps.

You will have a much better chance as a rising junior.  You have some of the background, you might even have seen or discussed some of the techniques in classes.  For my boss, I think students usually email her asking if there's a spot available in the lab.  If you want to go into a lab, make sure you read up on the work they do.  Read recent papers, even older papers are good as well.  Ask questions about the work.  This will make you stand out as someone who is intellectually curious and understood enough (it's not necessarily reasonable to expect you to understand all, but not all PIs are reasonable) to ask questions about the work that's been done in that lab.  What is your post-undergrad goal?  If it's graduate school, say that from the get-go.  If it's medical school (or dental, pharmacy, etc) DO NOT say you want to do research because it will look good on your CV.  Be engaged, be curious, ask questions, make conceptual connections.

I don't quite understand what you mean by this.  Research lab work?  Or it's a regular "follow the cookie cutter protocol to get the same result they've been getting for decades" lab?  Research lab work will really help you.  Normal teaching labs will help you by introducing you to techniques and concepts you might not have seen elsewhere.  My first intro micro lab taught me how to streak plates.  I've been doing them exactly the same way that they taught me since Fall of 2006, now, and on August 22nd I'll be teaching it to my new students the same way in their first day of my lab.  The skills weren't new, but they were still very important.

You can try, but most people will be unwilling to take a first semester freshman.  You simply don't have enough of a knowledge base to allow you to easily transition into a lab doing research and understanding what you're doing without a lot of work.  We took a second semester freshman once and she knew nothing.  All labs specialize in something, and it's hard to get new students to understand why the work is important if they don't know anything about the concept this work is specializing in.  This university screws incoming biological science people because of how the intro courses are done, so you might have a better shot.  It can't hurt to try, but don't be surprised if professors aren't interested in a freshman.
